subsystems.name: Framework Core
subsystems.description: Framework Core is the protocol-agnostic heart of Flask: it defines the app/blueprint scaffolding, configuration loading, context-local state, request/session proxies, helper utilities, logging, template dispatching, signals, type aliases, and class-based views. It exists as a distinct unit so that the WSGI-specific `Flask` class in src/flask/app.py and the CLI/testing layers can be built on top of a stable, reusable core without coupling routing, context, or template machinery to any particular server protocol. At request time, `AppContext.push` (src/flask/ctx.py:416) and `_AppCtxGlobals` (src/flask/ctx.py:30) establish the per-request state exposed through `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` proxies in src/flask/globals.py:41-62; routes and templates are wired earlier through `App.register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570), `Blueprint.register` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:273), and `Scaffold.add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376). Configuration enters via `Config.from_pyfile` (src/flask/config.py:187), `from_envvar` (src/flask/config.py:102), and `from_prefixed_env` (src/flask/config.py:126), while `helpers.url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200) and `templating.render_template` (src/flask/templating.py:136) tie URLs and templates back to the app. The core connects outward through related files such as src/flask/app.py, src/flask/cli.py, src/flask/json/provider.py, src/flask/sessions.py, src/flask/testing.py, and src/flask/wrappers.py, which compose these primitives into the concrete Flask runtime.

subsystems.name: Package API and Examples
subsystems.description: Package API and Examples contains the public package entry point `src/flask/__init__.py` together with the Celery, JavaScript, and tutorial example applications that exercise that API. It exists as a separate subsystem to demonstrate idiomatic application factories and blueprint usage so the framework's public contract is validated by realistic, runnable examples rather than only by unit tests. In the tutorial, `create_app` (examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py:6) builds the app, registers the auth and blog blueprints (examples/tutorial/flaskr/auth.py:16, examples/tutorial/flaskr/blog.py:13), and hooks `db.init_app` (examples/tutorial/flaskr/db.py:51) into the app context; the Celery example follows the same factory pattern through `create_app` and `celery_init_app` (examples/celery/src/task_app/__init__.py:7, examples/celery/src/task_app/__init__.py:29) and exposes tasks via the constants in examples/celery/make_celery.py:3 and examples/celery/make_celery.py:4. Data flows from HTTP views such as `views.add` (examples/celery/src/task_app/views.py:22) into Celery tasks (`tasks.add`, examples/celery/src/task_app/tasks.py:8) and back through `result` (examples/celery/src/task_app/views.py:11). The subsystem connects to the rest of Flask through related files including src/flask/app.py, src/flask/blueprints.py, src/flask/cli.py, src/flask/config.py, and src/flask/globals.py, which provide the framework features the examples invoke, with the test directories in related files using these apps as fixtures.

subsystems.name: Application Runtime
subsystems.description: The Application Runtime subsystem is Flask's central execution core: the Flask class in src/flask/app.py:110 owns the WSGI application object, route registration, configuration, and request dispatch, and the supporting modules in this cluster give that object its CLI, JSON, session, testing, and request/response plumbing. It exists as a separate cluster because every other Flask subsystem (blueprints, contexts, templating, signals) must coordinate through a single hub object rather than each managing its own lifecycle; isolating the core app object keeps that coordination in one place and lets extensions inject behavior through well-defined hooks. Control flow begins when a WSGI server calls Flask.wsgi_app (src/flask/app.py:1569), which enters a request context via request_context (src/flask/app.py:1504), calls full_dispatch_request (src/flask/app.py:995) to run preprocess/dispatch/finalize, and routes errors through handle_exception (src/flask/app.py:900). The CLI side starts from the cli constant in src/flask/cli.py:1110, locates and loads an app with find_app_by_string (src/flask/cli.py:120) and locate_app (src/flask/cli.py:241), then serves it. JSON responses flow through jsonify (src/flask/json/__init__.py:138) backed by DefaultJSONProvider (src/flask/json/provider.py:124), while sessions are opened and saved by SecureCookieSessionInterface (src/flask/sessions.py:284) using the tagged serializer in src/flask/json/tag.py:219. Testing is provided by FlaskClient (src/flask/testing.py:109), which reuses the normal app dispatch path through the open method (src/flask/testing.py:204). Through related files such as src/flask/__init__.py, blueprints.py, ctx.py, globals.py, helpers.py, sansio/app.py, and templating.py, this cluster both imports and is imported by the rest of the framework, so blueprints attach routes to the app, contexts are pushed around each request, and templates are rendered inside request handling.

overview.description: Flask is a Python web framework whose architecture separates a protocol-agnostic foundation, a concrete WSGI runtime, and the public package surface with runnable examples. The Framework Core supplies app/blueprint scaffolding, configuration, context-local proxies, template dispatching, and signals, while the Application Runtime builds on that core through the Flask class to provide WSGI dispatch, CLI, JSON, sessions, testing, and request/response plumbing. The Package API and Examples expose that functionality via the public package entry point and demonstrate it with application-factory and blueprint usage in Celery and tutorial apps. Together, the core's reusable primitives are orchestrated by the runtime, and the examples validate the resulting public API.
